name: Hana Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior copywriter at Greenhollow, a small oat-milk and plant yoghurt brand, and I lead a team of two. Mornings are planning: what's going on the cartons, the bus-shelter posters, the spring campaign. Afternoons I write, mostly by hand first in a yellow notebook, then I type it up. What wears me out is the sign-off chain, because a six-word line can bounce between four managers for a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and how does the money work out for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a line lands, like when we put 'Pour something kinder' on the carton and people started posting photos of it. The money is the bad part, honestly. Greenhollow pays below what bigger brands pay, and after rent on the flat I share with my partner Leon, a care-home nurse, I've got maybe two weeks of bills saved. There are only a couple of brands in this city that hire copywriters, so I can't just walk across the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like a relief. Nobody in the office talks about anything else, so a world where it fizzles out would be quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but nicely. In the team meeting I'd point out that our best-selling carton line came out of a notebook, not a chatbot. Online I'd probably share something about how creative work was never the easy thing to copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be nervous, because the money problem doesn't go away. Even if the robots don't take my job, Greenhollow could lose a supermarket listing and cut a post. And the routine stuff AI does take, like product descriptions for the website, is exactly what my junior Aisha does, so she's the one I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, writing by hand and pushing for fewer sign-off rounds. I'd try to put fifty a month into savings, which sounds tiny but is more than I manage now. I'd also go back to the creative workers' union meetings that I keep skipping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the work, but the rent sits on my chest either way. Picturing AI fizzle out is like being told the storm isn't coming while the roof still leaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Aisha. What would you actually say to her if the website descriptions went to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to fight to keep the parts that need a person, like the tasting days and talking to customers. I'd also tell my manager that if Aisha's hours get cut, I'm cutting mine in protest, though I'm not sure I could afford to. That's the honest bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money stays tight even in this calm picture, what gives first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership I barely use, then eating out with friends. Leon and I already batch-cook on Sundays. Saving fifty a month means no holiday this year, which stings, but we'd survive.

say: I'd tell the team our **best carton line** came from a notebook, not a chatbot.
I'd post that **creative work** was never as easy to copy as people claimed.
think: Privately, the **rent problem** stays even if AI fizzles out.
Greenhollow could still **lose a listing** and cut a post.
My junior's **routine copy** is exactly what AI would still take.
do: Keep writing **by hand** and push for fewer sign-off rounds.
Put **fifty a month** into savings, even if it means no holiday.
Go back to the **creative workers' union** meetings I keep skipping.
feel: Calm about the **craft** itself, but the thin savings still press on me.
S0.quote: Picturing AI fizzle out is like being told the storm isn't coming while the roof still leaks.
fieldNote: She is **relieved** by this picture but money worries don't lift at all.
Her protective instinct goes straight to her **junior colleague**, not herself.
She offers to cut her own hours in solidarity, then admits she **can't afford** it.

steps.text: Keep drafting carton and poster lines in her notebook first
Put fifty a month into a savings pot, skipping this year's holiday
Rejoin the monthly creative workers' union meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, that's the one I actually believe. Writing is the first thing on that list, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a proper agreement on how AI gets used before anyone signs a contract with a software company. Online I'd share the union's line about protecting creative jobs. I'd say it calmly, though, because I don't want to look like the one who's scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the one who's scared. I've never used these tools, not once, and I'd be the senior person on a team that's suddenly expected to churn out fifty ad versions a day. My manager Paul already asked in October whether we'd 'tried anything'. If Greenhollow decides one person with software can do what three of us do, I don't think I'm the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly and pay the dues, about twelve a month, and push for a workplace agreement. I'd ask Paul in writing what the plan is for our team, so it's on record. I'd probably look at whether there's a teaching route, like a short course to teach English or communication at the college, because I'd rather go somewhere people still matter than learn to babysit a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. It's like watching someone measure your desk for the next person. I'm angry too, because nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not learn the tools. If learning them kept your job, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep going back and forth. Part of me says just learn it, Hana, pay the rent. The other part of me thinks the moment I train the chatbot on my lines, I've written my own notice. I'd probably drag my feet until someone forced me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leon that night, if Paul told you the team was shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Leon we might need to move somewhere cheaper, maybe back near my mum. He'd say his care-home shifts can carry us for a bit, but they can't, not really. I'd probably cry in the shower so he didn't see.

say: I'd say we need a **written agreement** on AI before any software contract is signed.
I'd share the **union's line** online, calmly, so I don't look scared.
think: I've **never used** these tools and would be the oldest habit on the team.
If one person with software replaces three, I doubt **I'm kept**.
do: Join the union properly at **twelve a month** and push for an agreement.
Ask my manager **in writing** what the plan is for our team.
Look at a short course to **teach** communication at the college.
feel: **Sick** and watched, like someone measuring my desk.
**Angry** that nobody got a vote on this.
S1.quote: The moment I train the chatbot on my lines, I've written my own notice.
fieldNote: She is **openly torn** between learning the tools and refusing on principle.
Her public calm hides that she sees **herself** as first out.
Leaning on a **care-home nurse's** pay is her fallback, and she knows it won't hold.

steps.text: Pay union dues and push for a written AI agreement at Greenhollow
Ask her manager in writing what happens to the copy team
Look into a college course to teach communication
Talk with her partner about moving somewhere cheaper near her mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be twenty-nine. That's not a warning, that's a door slamming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say governments have to step in now, with a tax on the companies selling AI to fund people who lose work. I'd be at whatever protest there was. I'd say it loudly this time, because there's no point being polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my job is gone within a year of it arriving, maybe sooner. My work is all thinking work, words and screens, so I don't get the extra three years that Leon's job at the care home gets before the robots come. I'd have no savings, no plan, and Greenhollow would have no reason to keep a copywriter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know. I'd sign up for unemployment help the day I was let go and ask my mum if we could move into her spare room. I'd look at care work like Leon's, because hands-on jobs get a few more years, but I've no training for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. Like the floor's gone. I can't even picture what I'd be doing in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work gets a few more years. Would you really go into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Leon says the home is always short of carers, and nobody's building robots to hold someone's hand this year. But I'd be starting at the bottom on minimum pay with less than a month saved. Three more years in care work isn't a career, it's a waiting room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Greenhollow in this picture, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd probably keep the brand name and let software write everything. Paul would keep his job for a while because someone has to press the button. The thing that kills me is people would still buy the oat milk, and nobody would notice the words changed.

say: I'd say governments must **tax AI firms** now to fund people who lose work.
I'd **join the protests** and stop being polite about it.
think: My job is all **thinking work**, so it goes first, probably within a year.
With **no savings** and no plan, I'd have nothing to fall back on.
do: Sign up for **unemployment help** the day I'm let go.
Ask my mum about moving into her **spare room**.
Look at **care work** like my partner's, though I've no training.
feel: **Panicky**, like the floor has gone and 2029 is blank.
S2.quote: Three more years in care work isn't a career, it's a waiting room.
fieldNote: The **two-year** timeline leaves her without any plan she believes in.
She clearly sees that **hands-on** jobs get three more years, but doubts it helps.
Her anger turns to **politics**, while her own steps are survival moves.

steps.text: March and campaign for a tax on AI firms to fund lost jobs
Claim unemployment support the day Greenhollow lets her go
Move into her mum's spare room to stop paying rent
Ask the care home about entry-level carer shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, I suppose. I'd be thirty-two. Still young enough to start again, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window for unions and government to get ahead of it, with retraining money and limits on firing people for software. I'd write to my local representative. I'd tell friends this is the time to organise, not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd know my copywriting job has a shelf life of maybe four years. I'm bad at change, and I'd probably waste the first year hoping it was overblown. The extra time only helps if I actually use it, and I'm not sure I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself start a part-time teaching certificate in the first year, evenings, about two thousand spread over two years. I'd save hard, say a hundred a month, cutting eating out and the streaming services. I'd keep my job at Greenhollow as long as it lasts, because I need the wage to pay for the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dread, but a slower dread. Like knowing the exam date. There's a bit of hope in it too, that I could land somewhere people still need a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably waste the first year. What would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, someone else going first. I don't do new things alone, so I'd need my friend from the union to sign up first. If Rosa started a course, I'd sign up with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching, when AI can do thinking work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a classroom is part thinking and part being there with kids, and I think parents will want a person there for a long while. I could be wrong. But it's the only thing I can picture myself doing that still feels like mine.

say: I'd call this the **window** for unions and government to act.
I'd **write to my representative** about retraining money and firing limits.
think: My copywriting job has maybe **four years** left.
I'd likely **waste the first year** hoping it was overblown.
do: Start a part-time **teaching certificate** in evenings, about two thousand.
Save **a hundred a month** by cutting eating out and streaming.
Keep the **Greenhollow wage** as long as it lasts to fund the course.
feel: A slower **dread**, like knowing the exam date.
A thread of **hope** about a job that still needs a person.
S3.quote: I don't do new things alone, so I'd need my friend from the union to sign up first.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a **plan**, but she doubts she'd act on it in time.
She picks teaching because it mixes thinking with **being in the room**.
Her biggest driver to change is **company**, not information.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening teaching certificate with a friend
Save a hundred a month by cancelling streaming and eating in
Write to her local representative asking for retraining funds
Stay at Greenhollow as long as the wage lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole other life away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse now for leaving people behind. A decade is enough time to build proper retraining and a safety net. I'd say that at work and online, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years lets me keep my head in the sand for a while, which is my worst habit. I'd probably carry on at Greenhollow for five or six years and only move when I had to. Leon and I might finally want kids in that time, and I don't know how we'd plan for that with my job on a timer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, honestly, not much. I'd keep my job, pay into the union, and save what I could, maybe seventy a month. I'd look at the teaching course but probably put it off to year three or four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened yet. The worry is that I'd feel fine for too long, and then suddenly it's 2035 and I'm still writing carton copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would make me wait. I couldn't have a baby on my salary with no savings and a job that's going to vanish. Leon wants them sooner, so we'd argue about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd waste the first year. With ten years, what would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deadline I can see. If Greenhollow announced a date for switching to AI copy, I'd move that week. Without one, I'd drift, and I know it.

say: I'd say a **decade** is enough time to build retraining and a safety net.
I'd tell people there's **no excuse** for leaving anyone behind.
think: Ten years lets me **bury my head**, which is my worst habit.
Planning for **kids** with my job on a timer feels impossible.
do: Stay at **Greenhollow** and keep paying union dues.
Save about **seventy a month** in the first year.
Push the **teaching course** back to year three or four.
feel: Uneasy rather than frightened, with fear of **drifting** too long.
S4.quote: I couldn't have a baby on my salary with no savings and a job that's going to vanish.
fieldNote: More time makes her **less likely** to act early, and she knows it.
The real cost she names is **delaying children**, not the job itself.
She needs an **outside deadline** to move.

steps.text: Keep writing for Greenhollow and paying union dues
Save about seventy a month from the first year
Put off trying for children until her income is clearer
Wait until year three before signing up for teaching

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and no money to do anything except panic. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, paid for by the firms making the money. And a union that's already in the building, not one we start after the layoffs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets to decide. Everyone talks about AI like weather, like it just happens. Somebody signs the software contract, and I'd like those people asked the questions you're asking me.

headlineQuote: Somebody signs the software contract, and I'd like those people asked the questions you're asking me.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old** senior copywriter at a small oat-milk brand, writing by hand first.
She has **under a month** of savings and few local jobs to move to.
She refuses AI tools on principle, then admits she **fears** being first out.
Faster pictures push her from union organising toward **panic**, care work and her mum's spare room.
With ten years she would likely **drift**, delaying children until her income feels safe.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time or money to do anything but panic.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** during retraining, paid for by the firms profiting from AI.
A **union** already in the building before layoffs start.
